transcript.content: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you for seeing me. I, um... I came in because I just can't seem to get anything in order anymore. It's like everything is slipping through my fingers. You see, my kitchen table—which used to be where we'd have our nice Sunday breakfasts, just me and my husband—is completely covered now. I mean, you can't even see the wood underneath. It's just piles and piles of his medical appointment papers, because he's been having some trouble with his knee, and then there are all these church flyers for the bake sale and the choir schedule, and notes from the senior center about the Tuesday bingo and the Wednesday walking group... and all these half-finished lists I make. I write them thinking, "Okay, this will help," but I only get halfway through before I lose my train of thought. So I just sit there at the table, looking at all of it, and I honestly don't know which thing to do first. I pick up a paper, put it down, look at another one... and before I know it, the whole day is gone. Just gone. And I haven't accomplished a single thing. It's so frustrating because I feel like I should be able to handle this, but I just sit there paralyzed by it all.
Have you struggled with staying organized and focused throughout your life, or is this a recent change for you?

Oh, well, you know, my husband asked me that very same thing just the other day when I lost his prescription slip again. He thought maybe it was just my age, you know, being seventy and all, but I... I really don't think it's just getting older. If I'm being completely honest, and I've been thinking about this a lot lately, it's always been this way. Always. I mean, going all the way back to when I was a little girl in grade school. 

My mother kept all my old report cards in this beautiful cedar chest—which I still have, actually, it's sitting at the foot of the guest bed right now, though it's completely covered in laundry I haven't folded yet—but anyway, I was looking through those old report cards a few years back. And every single year, the teachers would write the exact same thing in the margins. They'd say I was a bright girl, very sweet, but just so careless. That was the word they always used, careless. I was constantly forgetting my textbooks at school, or I'd leave my homework on the kitchen counter after I'd spent all evening agonizing over it. 

I remember Mrs. Gable—she was my third-grade teacher, such a strict woman with these thick horn-rimmed glasses—she wrote a whole long note to my parents about how she constantly had to stand over my desk and give me reminders to finish my seatwork. Because if she didn't, I'd just stare out the window at the trees or daydream about whatever came into my head, and she wouldn't let me go outside for recess until the worksheet was done. So I'd be stuck inside while everyone else was out playing jump rope or tag. It was just awful. It's like my brain has always been a little bit like a butterfly, just fluttering away from whatever I'm supposed to be doing. So no, it's not new at all, it's just... maybe it feels heavier now because there's so much more paperwork in life, you know? When you're a child, someone else manages the big things, but now it's all on me, and I just can't seem to keep up with it.

latest_inference.note: Childhood onset of marked inattention, daydreaming, disorganization, and forgetfulness confirmed through school records rules out late-onset cognitive disorder (F06.7), primary mood disorder (F32), primary anxiety disorder (F41.1), and obsessive-compulsive/hoarding disorder (F42), pointing definitively to lifelong ADHD.
